Pool frog embryos developing within their gelatinous egg masses at a constant laboratory temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] typically complete eclosion after 8 days [ab = 8 days], a developmental pace that aligns with rates observed in other European water frogs of the genus Pelophylax. Upon hatching, the newly emerged tadpoles measure approximately 0.89 cm [Lb = approximately 0.89 cm] in total length, reflecting the modest size of the yolk-dependent, pre-feeding larva. The wet weight at this neonatal stage is remarkably slight, averaging only 0.0063 grams [Wwb = 0.0063 grams], a value that underscores the lecithotrophic nature of the earliest larval phase before the onset of exogenous feeding. This combination of a brief embryonic period and a small initial body size is interpreted as an adaptation to ephemeral breeding ponds, where rapid hatching enhances offspring survival before desiccation or predation pressure intensifies. Field surveys of natural spawning sites corroborate these laboratory findings, suggesting that the thermal regime of shallow, sun-exposed pools closely matches the incubation conditions under which these developmental parameters were established.

The aquatic tadpole phase of Pelophylax lessonae proceeds through a predictable sequence of Gosner stages characterized by steady somatic growth. Under controlled conditions maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the time since birth at metamorphosis is 120 days , a relatively protracted larval duration that reflects the cool thermal regimen typical of the species' northern range margins. By the time they reach metamorphic climax, tadpoles attain a total length of 6.5 cm , a dimension that encompasses both body and tail components prior to tail resorption. At this same developmental transition, the snout-vent length of the newly metamorphosed froglet is 1.9 cm , marking the onset of the terrestrial juvenile stage. The wet weight at metamorphosis averages 0.65 grams , representing a substantial increase from the hatchling mass. This tenfold gain in body mass over the course of larval development is consistent with the energetic demands of building the musculoskeletal and organ systems necessary for terrestrial locomotion and air breathing.

As post-metamorphic juveniles transition into the sub-adult phase, growth continues at a decelerating rate until the attainment of sexual maturity. For female Pool frogs, the time since metamorphosis at puberty is 730 days [tp = 730 days], a value recorded at a standard environmental temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. At the onset of gonadal maturation, individuals reach a total length of 3.9 cm [Lp = 3.9 cm], a body size that correlates closely with the initiation of reproductive activity in field populations. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 7 grams [Wwp = 7 grams], representing approximately one-sixth of the maximum mass attained by fully grown adults. This inflection point in the growth trajectory is linked to the allocation of resources toward gametogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics such as the lateral vocal sacs in males. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this size at maturity is conservative, possibly reflecting the constraints of a short active season in temperate European habitats.

Fully grown adult Pool frogs exhibit a maximum recorded ultimate total length of 7.6 cm [Li = 7.6 cm], a value that places them among the smaller representatives of the Pelophylax esculentus complex. The ultimate wet weight of reproductively active adults reaches 41.3 grams [Wwi = 41.3 grams], a mass that is partitioned between somatic tissue and, in gravid females, the developing egg mass. Longevity under natural conditions is estimated at 6 years [am = 6 years] when assessed at a sustained temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], though some museum records hint at the possibility of slightly older individuals in undisturbed populations. This lifespan is moderate for a ranid frog of this body size, falling between the shorter-lived explosive breeders and the longer-lived montane specialists. The balance between adult survival and annual reproductive output appears to be a key determinant of population persistence in the dynamic pond landscapes that characterize the species' preferred habitat.

Reproductive phenology in Pelophylax lessonae is tightly linked to spring temperature regimes and photoperiodic cues. Observations of gravid females in breeding aggregations indicate that individuals attain an adult body condition that permits the production of a single clutch of eggs per year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs per year], with typical clutch sizes averaging around 700 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = around 700 eggs per clutch]. The interval between successive spawning events within a single season is generally not observed, as females in northern populations typically deposit only one egg mass annually. This modest reproductive frequency is compensated by the relatively high fecundity per event, ensuring that even a single successful breeding season can contribute substantially to recruitment. The species' reliance on ephemeral water bodies means that the timing of oviposition is critical, and females often deposit their eggs within days of the first sustained warm spell in early May, synchronizing larval development with peak zooplankton abundance.
